levels.foilDesignLogic: Each foil differs from the audio target by exactly ONE phoneme, placed at a different position (onset / vowel / coda), so the child must check every sound. Foils are mostly real CVC neighbours because the CVC neighbourhood is dense; a few visual (b/d) and L1-tagged foils (r/l, final voicing) are included.
levels.researchRationale: Beginning spellers represent initial and final consonants before medial vowels (Read, 1971; Treiman, 1993). Placing the contrast at each position trains full-word sound-to-letter mapping (Ehri, 2005: partial to full alphabetic phase). b/d letter-form confusions are common at ages 5-7 (Treiman, 1993).

levels.foilDesignLogic: Each item: (a) a cluster-omission foil (stop > sop), (b) a vowel foil, (c) a coda substitution (often a voicing or nasal contrast). S-cluster items swap in an L1 prothesis/epenthesis foil.
levels.researchRationale: Beginners often drop the second consonant of an onset cluster and the nasal before a final stop (Bruck & Treiman, 1990; Treiman, 1993), so omission foils reflect authentic spelling errors. L1 vowel insertion or prothesis is a documented transfer pattern (Swan & Smith, 2001).

levels.skillPattern: Consonant digraphs (sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ng, nk)
levels.foilDesignLogic: Foils include: a rival digraph (sh/ch), a single-letter omission of the digraph, a vowel foil, and for ck / ng / nk a phonetically-plausible or contrast form. L1 th substitutions (t, d, s) replace one foil on th words.
levels.researchRationale: A digraph functions as one grapheme; learners must treat two letters as one unit (Ehri, 2005). ck > k appears here as the first pseudohomophone because ck is a positional orthographic convention (Kessler & Treiman, 2001).

levels.foilDesignLogic: First level where foils include PSEUDOHOMOPHONES (kake, maik). Also: missing-e foil (cak = short vowel reading) and a wrong-vowel + e foil.
levels.researchRationale: Once children read decodable words reliably, spelling choice tasks with phonologically equivalent alternatives separate orthographic knowledge from phonological decoding (Olson et al., 1994; Share, 1995). Children invent spellings such as kake / maik before learning conventional patterns (Read, 1971; Treiman, 1993).

levels.skillPattern: Vowel teams (ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, ow, oo, igh)
levels.foilDesignLogic: Vowel-team words: a pseudohomophone with an alternate spelling of the same vowel (bote, leef), a short-vowel omission foil, and a wrong-team or letter-order foil (oa > ao).
levels.researchRationale: English long vowels have several possible spellings; the correct team is often position- or word-specific (Kessler & Treiman, 2001), so only orthographic knowledge separates the target from the pseudohomophone. Position-constraint errors (ao) show whether letter order is stored (Treiman & Bourassa, 2000).

levels.foilDesignLogic: R-controlled and diphthong items: r omission, an alternate r-controlled spelling (bird > burd), wrong vowel, and diphthong swaps (oi/oy, ow/ou).
levels.researchRationale: Vowel + r and diphthongs have many spellings; the same-sound alternatives (er/ir/ur) are the classic hard spellings (Bear et al., Words Their Way). Omitting r also reflects non-rhotic varieties, so record audio with a clear /r/.

levels.skillPattern: Irregular high-frequency words, silent letters, soft c/g
levels.foilDesignLogic: Irregular high-frequency words (Dolch / Fry): regularized spelling (sed, wuz), letter-order foil (was > saw), and omission. Silent letters (kn, mb) and soft c/g: pseudohomophones (fase, caje).
levels.researchRationale: High-frequency irregular words must be learned as specific letter sequences; regularizations are the typical error (Ehri, 2005; Treiman, 1993). Word list based on Dolch (1936) and Fry (1980).

levels.foilDesignLogic: Inflection and suffix items: sound-based spelling of the suffix (jumpt, dogz), missing or excess doubling, keep-e / no y>i changes (makeing, babys), -full for -ful.
levels.researchRationale: Children rely on sound for suffixes until morphological knowledge develops (Treiman & Cassar, 1996; Nunes, Bryant & Bindman, 1997). Double letters are learned early as an orthographic pattern (Cassar & Treiman, 1997).

levels.foilDesignLogic: Two-syllable and longer words: unstressed-vowel substitution, syllable omission, letter transposition, doubling errors, pseudohomophone (pensil, elefant).
levels.researchRationale: Unstressed (schwa) vowels are phonologically ambiguous, so spelling must draw on orthographic memory; syllable-level omission and transposition foils reflect real errors (Treiman & Bourassa, 2000).

levels.skillPattern: Advanced patterns (-tion, ough, ch=/k/, ph/gh, etc.)
levels.foilDesignLogic: Low-consistency patterns (-tion, ough, gh/ph = /f/, ch = /k/, sc = /s/). Foils are mostly pseudohomophones that follow more-regular mappings.
levels.researchRationale: The most opaque spellings are where phonologically plausible alternatives are most tempting; distractors built from plausible errors discriminate best (Haladyna, Downing & Rodriguez, 2002).

foilCodebook.name: Initial-consonant substitution
foilCodebook.definition: Onset differs by one phoneme from the target.
foilCodebook.probe: Attention to the first sound; grapheme-phoneme mapping at word start

foilCodebook.name: Final-consonant substitution
foilCodebook.definition: Coda differs by one phoneme (often place or voicing contrast).
foilCodebook.probe: Attention to the last sound; end-of-word phoneme segmentation

foilCodebook.name: Vowel substitution
foilCodebook.definition: Medial vowel replaced by a different vowel letter with a different sound.
foilCodebook.probe: Vowel grapheme-phoneme mapping (vowels are the last position children master)

foilCodebook.name: Visual-confusable letter
foilCodebook.definition: Target letter replaced by a mirror/rotation twin (b/d, p/q, m/w, n/u).

foilCodebook.name: Omission
foilCodebook.definition: A grapheme (cluster member, final letter, silent letter, r, e, vowel) is dropped so the string no longer represents all the sounds or the pattern.
foilCodebook.probe: Phonemic completeness (cluster reduction) and knowledge of orthographic patterns (silent e)

foilCodebook.name: Digraph confusion
foilCodebook.definition: One digraph replaced with a neighbouring digraph.
foilCodebook.probe: Treating two letters as one grapheme; sh/ch/th contrasts

foilCodebook.name: Transposition / reversal
foilCodebook.definition: Two adjacent letters swapped, or a whole-word reversal.

foilCodebook.name: Pseudohomophone (phonologically plausible misspelling)
foilCodebook.definition: Non-word (or rare form) that sounds identical to the target when decoded but is not the conventional spelling.
foilCodebook.probe: Orthographic knowledge beyond phonics; the 'orthographic choice' logic

foilCodebook.name: Regularization
foilCodebook.definition: An irregular word spelled the way its sounds would be spelled by the most typical rules.
foilCodebook.probe: Word-specific (lexical) spelling memory for irregular words

foilCodebook.name: Over-generalization / wrong pattern
foilCodebook.definition: A legitimate English pattern applied where it does not belong (wrong vowel team, keep-e, -full, -ed as -id, no y>i change).
foilCodebook.probe: Rule and morphology knowledge; pattern position constraints

foilCodebook.name: Doubling error
foilCodebook.probe: Knowledge of consonant doubling in short-vowel + suffix contexts

foilCodebook.name: L1 transfer: /r/-/l/ confusion
foilCodebook.definition: Onset r and l swapped. Common in learners whose L1 has one liquid phoneme or a different r/l contrast.
foilCodebook.probe: Language-specific phonology (e.g., some East Asian and Bantu L1 backgrounds). Swan & Smith (2001)

foilCodebook.name: L1 transfer: final devoicing
foilCodebook.definition: Final voiced stop written as voiceless (d>t) where L1 lacks final voiced obstruents.

foilCodebook.name: L1 transfer: prothetic vowel before s-cluster
foilCodebook.probe: Spanish, Hindi/Urdu and other L1s where s-clusters are not permitted word-initially. Swan & Smith (2001)

foilCodebook.name: L1 transfer: epenthesis in a cluster
foilCodebook.definition: Vowel inserted between consonants of a cluster.
foilCodebook.probe: L1s with simple CV syllable structure (many Bantu languages). Swan & Smith (2001)

foilCodebook.name: L1 transfer: th substitution
foilCodebook.definition: /th/ replaced by t, d or s where L1 lacks dental fricatives.
foilCodebook.probe: Hindi/Urdu, Hausa, Arabic, French, and other L1 backgrounds. Swan & Smith (2001)

foilCodebook.name: L1 transfer: short/long vowel merger
foilCodebook.probe: L1s with a single high front vowel (e.g., Spanish, many South Asian languages). Swan & Smith (2001)

researchNotes: How the foils were designed

1. Every foil is an error a learner could plausibly make. Multiple-choice distractors work best when they are built from common errors and are plausible to learners who lack the target knowledge (Haladyna, Downing & Rodriguez, 2002). Foils here are drawn from documented invented-spelling and phonics-error patterns, not random letter changes.

2. Foil difficulty rises with the learner's developmental phase (Ehri, 2005). Levels 1-3 foils are phonologically DIFFERENT from the audio (a decoder can reject them). From Level 4 on, one or more foils are pseudohomophones that sound like the target, so only orthographic knowledge can reject them (the orthographic choice logic of Olson et al., 1994).
3. Position balance. In Levels 1-3 the contrast is spread across onset, vowel, and coda so the child cannot succeed by attending to only the first letter.

4. No foil is a homophone of its target (checked against the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary). Where a natural foil was a real homophone (tale, sea, not, sum, won, wood), it was excluded or the target was swapped.

5. Real-word foils are limited and flagged (WordList column L), because a real word can pull a child toward meaning. Pseudohomophones are treated as non-words even where a rare or web-slang form exists (e.g., 'yu').

6. L1-transfer foils are tagged (codes beginning 'L1-'). They replace a general foil on selected items, so the game can serve either the general foil or the L1 foil by learner profile. They are keyed to documented interference patterns (Swan & Smith, 2001); confirm against your target languages (e.g., Hausa, Swahili, Hindi/Urdu) before use.

7. Word selection: words are high-frequency or decodable, use age-appropriate vocabulary for 5-8 year olds, and cover the spelling patterns in the level order of the Words Their Way and structured-literacy scope-and-sequences. Irregular words come from Dolch (1936) and Fry (1980).
8. Progression: consistent CVC > blends > digraphs > silent e > vowel teams > r-controlled/diphthongs > irregular/silent-letter > inflections > multisyllable > opaque patterns.
Suggested game use
- Randomize position of the correct answer on every trial. Do not reuse one foil slot for one type.
- Adaptive option: use Tier 1-2 foils (IC, FC, V, VIS, DIG) when the child is unsure; unlock Tier 3-4 foils (PH, REG, OVR, DBL) after accuracy passes a threshold at the same level.
- Distractor analysis after pilot: retire any foil chosen by <5% of respondents in a level and replace it; revisit any foil chosen more often than the correct answer.
- Record audio in the dialect the children hear. Check items that depend on vowel mergers (pin/pen, cot/caught, r-dropping, wh/w) for your target audience.
Cautions
- This list is a research-informed DRAFT; it has not been piloted. Foil selection rates and difficulty ordering should be checked empirically.
- Pronunciation assumptions are General American. Some foils may be ambiguous in other varieties (e.g., 'hows' for house, r-omission foils in non-rhotic accents).
- References were cited from memory of the literature; please verify volume and page details before formal publication.
